source_text: Ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἑξῆς κατηγορῶν τῆς Μω(??)σέως ἱστορίας αἰτιᾶται τοὺς τροπολογοῦντας καὶ ἀλληγοροῦντας αὐτήν. ἦν δ᾿ ἂν εἰπεῖν πρὸς τὸν γενναιότατον καὶ ἀληθῆ λόγον ἐπιγράψαντα τὸ ἑαυτοῦ βιβλίον. τί δήποτε. ὦ οὗτος. θεοὺς μὲν τηλικαύταις περιπίπτοντας συμφοραῖς. ὁποίας ἀναγράφουσιν οἱ σοφοί σου ποιηταὶ καὶ φιλόσοφοι, καὶ ἐναγέσι μίξεσι χρωμένους καὶ κατὰ τῶν πατέρων στρατευομένους καὶ τὰ αἰδοῖα αὐτῶν ἀποτέμνοντας σεμνολογεῖς ἀναγεγράφθαι τὰ τηλικαῦτα τετολμηκέναι καὶ πεποιηκέναι καὶ πεπονθέναι· ὅταν δὲ Μω(??)σῆς μὴ περὶ θεοῦ τοιαῦτα λέγῃ ἀλλὰ μηδ᾿ ἀγγέλων ἁγίων περὶ δὲ ἀνθρώπων πολλῷ ἐλάττονα (οὐδεὶς γὰρ παρ᾿ αὐτῷ ἐτόλμησεν ὅσα Κρόνος κατὰ τοῦ Οὐρανοῦ οὐδ᾿ ὅσα Ζεὺς κατὰ τοῦ πατρὸς, οὐδ᾿ ὅτι τῇ ἑαυτοῦ θυγατρὶ ὁ „πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε“ συνελήλυθεν), πλανᾶν νομίζετε ἠπατημένους τοὺς νενομοθετημένους ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ; δοκεῖ δὲ μοι καὶ παραπλήσιόν τι Κέλσος ποιεῖν τῷ Πλατωνικῷ Θρασυμάχῳ, μὴ ἐπιτρέποντι ὡς βούλεται ἀποκρίνασθαι περὶ τῆς δικαιοσύνης Σωκράτει ἀλλὰ λέγοντι· ὅρα μὴ τὸ συμφέρον εἴπῃς εἶναι τὸ δίκαιον μηδὲ τὸ δέον μηδ᾿ ἄλλο τι τῶν παραπλησίων. καὶ γὰρ οὗτος κατηγορήσας, ὡς οἴεται. τῶν παρὰ Μωϋσεῖ ἱστοριῶν καὶ μεμψάμενος τοῖς ἀλληγοροῦσι μετὰ τοῦ καὶ ἔπαινόν τινα περὶ αὐτῶν λέγειν, ὅτι εἰσὶν οἱ ἐπιεικέστεροι. οἱονεὶ κωλύεται κατηγορήσας, ὡς βούλεται, ἀπολογεῖσθαι τοὺς δυναμένους. ὡς πέφυκεν ἔχειν τὰ πράγματα.
thought_title: Critique of Celsus' View on Moses' History
pass_a_gloss: But in the following, accusing the history of Moses, he blames those who interpret it tropologically and allegorically. It would have been fitting to say to the most noble and truthful word writer of his own book, what then, oh this one, you consider the gods, who fall into such great misfortunes, as your wise poets and philosophers write, and who engage in shameful mixings and wage war against their fathers and cut off their private parts, to be recorded as having dared and done and suffered such great things; but when Moses does not speak about such things concerning God, nor even about holy angels, but about people, and much lesser things (for no one among them dared as much as Kronos against Ouranos, nor as much as Zeus against his father, nor that the 'father of men and gods' had intercourse with his own daughter), do you think you deceive those who have been legislated by him? It seems to me that Celsus does something similar to the Platonic Thrasymachus, who does not allow Socrates to answer as he wishes about justice, but says: 'see that you do not say that the advantageous is the just, nor the necessary, nor anything else similar.' And this one, having accused, as he thinks, the histories according to Moses, and having found fault with those who allegorize, even praises some of them for saying that they are more gentle, as if he is prevented, having accused as he wishes, from defending those who are able. As is natural for things to be.
pass_b_english: Next, Celsus attacks the Mosaic history by blaming those who read it tropologically and allegorically. One could fairly ask the noble and truthful author of his own book: "Why do you dignify as divine beings figures who suffer such great misfortunes, as your wise poets and philosophers record — engaging in shameful unions, waging war against their fathers, even castrating themselves — and then record that they dared, did, and endured such things? Yet when Moses speaks, he does not attribute such acts to God, nor even to holy angels, but only to human beings, and far lesser offenses at that. No one in his account dared what Kronos did to Ouranos, or Zeus to his father, or what the 'father of men and gods' did with his own daughter. Do you really think you are deceiving the people he gave laws to?"

Celsus strikes me as doing much the same thing as the Platonic Thrasymachus, who would not let Socrates answer about justice on his own terms but insisted, "See that you do not claim the advantageous is the just, nor the necessary, nor anything like them." Celsus first accuses, as he supposes, the histories in Moses and faults the allegorizers, yet he even praises some of them for being more moderate — as if, having accused as he wishes, he could then bar those who are able from offering a defense. That is simply how things stand.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the parenthetical comparison to Kronos and Zeus, the reference to Thrasymachus, and the final clause regarding the natural state of things. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.
